title: Joy opens the heart
hookLine: Hasidism treats joy as a spiritual force, sadness as a closing

cards: A hand that is clenched can't receive anything. Try it right now if you like: make a fist, and then try to take a cup from someone. You can't.
You have to open first. Yesterday's word asked how a person holds on to God all day long. Underneath it sits another question: what keeps a person from holding on?
Hasidic teaching points somewhere you might not look first. Sadness. Heaviness.
The gray mood that closes the hand. And the thing that opens it again is today's word.

teach.b: Simcha. Joy, gladness, the word wedding guests use when they wish a family more simchas. First, the verse.
The psalm says, "Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing." Notice that gladness isn't the reward at the end of the service. It is the way the service is done.
Second, the Talmud. In tractate Shabbat the sages teach that the Divine Presence does not rest on a person in the middle of sadness or laziness, but in the middle of the joy of a mitzvah.

teach.h: A MOOD CAN BE A DOOR OR A WALL.
teach.b: Read that way, a mood can be a door, or a wall. Third, the Hasidic turn. The early Hasidic teachers took that teaching and made it central.
Joy, for them, isn't a feeling you wait for.

teach.h: JOY AS A FORCE THAT OPENS.
teach.b: It's a force, something that opens the heart so prayer can go up and blessing can come down.
Sadness, in their language, is a closing, a contraction, and they treated it as something to work against, not something to admire. Fourth, and this matters: they didn't mean pretending.
Hasidic teachers made a careful distinction.

teach.h: A BROKEN HEART IS NOT A CLOSED ONE.
teach.b: A broken heart, honest sorrow over a wrong you did, they valued. That kind of sorrow moves you.
What they warned against was the heavy, stuck sadness that only sits there and closes everything. One is a door being knocked on. The other is a door locked from inside.
So simcha isn't the absence of pain. It's the hand staying open, even in a hard week.

how: In Hasidic communities joy is cultivated on purpose: singing wordless melodies called niggunim, dancing at weddings and festivals, and teaching that a mitzvah done gladly is done fully.

o: a gift given at a wedding or a bar mitzvah
joy, a force that opens the heart to God
a calm with no feelings, high or low

p: the Presence rests in the joy of a mitzvah

s: Hasidic teachers said all sorrow is bad
they valued a broken heart over a real wrong. what they warned against was heavy, stuck sadness.
in the psalm, gladness is the way the service is done
"serve the LORD with gladness": joy isn't the prize at the end, it's the manner.
simcha means pretending to be happy
the teachers meant an open heart, not a mask over pain.

games.q: you're in a gray, heavy week. a Hasidic teacher would say the first thing to work on is:
o: the heaviness itself, because it closes the heart.
nothing, wait until the mood passes.
games.why: they treated stuck sadness as a closing, something to work against, because joy is what opens the heart to prayer.

practice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up, and look for one thing in your life right now that is good: warm socks, a message from a friend, coffee still hot.
Stay with it without explaining it away or adding a but, and notice whether anything in your chest loosens. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words, serve the LORD with gladness, and let them sit.

wordCard.voice: Simcha. Joy, gladness. For the Hasidic teachers, a spiritual force that opens the heart, where heavy sadness closes it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness. Also the everyday word for a happy family occasion.

carryVoice: Your line: joy opens. A broken heart, the Hasidic teachers said, is not a closed one. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing.
